extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly; educated public interested in science, law, and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Magazine-essay analysis arguing for making telegraph service part of the general postal system in the United States, assessing constitutional authority, foreign experience, and likely benefits/financials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional right to own and operate telegraph lines
rubrics_metrics.description: That clause of the Constitution (section 8 of Article I: 'Congress shall have power ... to establish post-offices and post-roads') grants the General Government authority to regulate and conduct the transmission of intelligence, including by improved methods such as the telegraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by Supreme Court language (Pensacola Telegraph Co. v. Western Union) that powers 'keep pace with the progress of the country' and extend to new agencies (horse → stagecoach → railroad → telegraph). The framers intended the interchange of intelligence, not just then-existing instrumentalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional duty to include telegraph in the postal system
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only a right but a constitutional duty of the Government to make the telegraph part of the general postal system, to the exclusion of private competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument rests on the absolute nature of powers granted to the General Government (tenth amendment reasoning) and citations (ex parte Jackson) that Congress's power 'embraces the regulation of the entire postal system of the country.' It is presented as inconsistent to enforce monopoly for slower methods while leaving the telegraph to private monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical test: success in other countries
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether governmental control has proved a success in other countries where postal telegraphs have been organized (Belgium, Switzerland, France, Great Britain, Russia, Germany, Sweden, Italy, New Zealand, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay supplies empirical evidence (years of adoption, tariffs, receipts, expenses, number of offices and miles of line) showing net revenues and public benefit. The 'registered system' (double fee for an exact copy and time of delivery) and reductions in tariff over time are given as examples of successful organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective test: likely beneficial results in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: That a beneficial result is likely to follow from adopting government control in the United States, given national energy, enterprise, and extent of the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends a uniform tariff (example: twenty cents for twenty words or less) and argues such a tariff could cover expenses in a few years or become a revenue source. This criterion ties legal permissibility and foreign success to domestic practicability and finance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-benefit criterion: protect citizens from monopolies and assure privacy/efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Government operation would protect citizens from extortions of monopolies and guarantee for a small charge the transmission and delivery of telegraphic correspondence with the privacy of sealed letters, with greater certainty and efficiency than private corporations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a normative standard for judging the desirability of public control; supported by comparison to private rates, delays, and inaccurate rendering that prompted British Chambers of Commerce to favor postal telegraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of constitutional interpretation adapting to new technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers granted in the Constitution are not confined to instrumentalities known at adoption but adapt to new developments; therefore postal power extends to telegraphy and other modern agencies of communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Supreme Court reasoning enumerating historical progressions of transport/communication (horse → stage-coach → steamboat → railroad → telegraph); used as legal justification for including telegraph within postal authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation on tariff as an evaluative/implementation detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a uniform tariff (example proposed: twenty cents for twenty words or less) as part of making a postal telegraph system financially viable and equitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cites foreign tariff reductions and domestic receipts/expenses to justify a uniform low rate that would increase usage, cover costs, and protect citizens; the specific numeric example is given as a policy lever to test viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific method as a standard for biblical criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Science properly means a method of investigation (not just facts) and therefore the Christian Scriptures should be subjected to scientific methods—tests of reason, reinvestigation, and higher standards of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor argues that applying the scientific method to biblical criticism (as in the revised New Testament and Robertson Smith's work) is appropriate and beneficial; this is offered as a normative evaluative principle for scholarship rather than as a threat to faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly-critical balance: apply criticism without abandoning essential faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical scholarship should subject texts to reasoned inquiry and recognize human and imperfect aspects, while not necessarily undermining essential religious truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented via Robertson Smith's position: he applies critical history to parts of the Bible, maintains essential truth, and treats the Bible as a book of 'experimental religion'—a model for how critical methods can coexist with religious commitment.
